processing: Typical of raw pu-erh from Bada: sun-dried green leaf (maocha), sold loose or pressed, with no ripe-style piling.
harvest_season: As usual across Menghai, spring picking is the prized one.
appearance_dry: As with other Bada large-leaf raw pu-erh, long dark olive leaves with some pale buds.
appearance_liquor: Typically clear gold when young, as with Bada raw pu-erh.
appearance_wet: Typically thick, large olive-green leaves, as with other Yunnan large-leaf tea.
taste_profile: Nothing specific to Hesong is well recorded. Bada tea as a whole is described as strong, with pronounced bitterness and astringency, a lasting sweet finish, and plum and honey aromas.

brewing.notes: Bada teas can be firmly bitter, so start with a slightly lighter dose and very short steeps.

vintage_note: Like other raw pu-erh, it is sold by harvest year, usually spring material pressed the same year. Hesong rarely appears as a named product; Bada tea is more often sold under the mountain's name or blended, so a village label deserves a question about where the leaf came from.
description:
Hesong is a village on Bada Mountain, at the southern end of Menghai County near the Myanmar border. Tea people know the name mostly because of one tree, not because of a recognised style in the cup.

The area has both cultivated trees and wild large-leaf tea forest. Processing would follow the usual raw pu-erh route, with sun-drying and no ripe-style piling.

Little is recorded about Hesong's own flavour. Bada tea in general is strong, with real bitterness and astringency, a lasting sweetness, and plum and honey in the aroma, so brew it lightly at first.

Be careful with any product that trades on the famous tree. The tree's fame belongs to one wild specimen, and it tells you nothing about the leaf in a given cake.
history:
Hesong's place in tea writing comes from the so-called king of wild tea trees near the village. Reported figures for it put its age at about 1,700 to 1,800 years, and one account gives a height of 34 metres; these ages are estimates repeated in the trade, and accounts even disagree on whether the tree counts as wild or cultivated.

Little else is documented about tea-making in the village itself.
